rationale: A is more coherent and actionable: it defines when queued benchmark work may trigger a model swap, uses explicit hysteresis, separates model-bound cache tiers, and reconciles a paged allocator with a memory ledger. B has useful cancellation and watchdog details, but its policy never clearly transitions to a benchmark’s nonresident model, its sticky mode can block interactive traffic regardless of urgency, its admission estimate omits output-token KV growth, and its claim that the ledger—not the real allocator—is authoritative is unsafe. A still overstates guarantees such as never rejecting interactive requests and treats CPU KV offload as more universally practical than it is, but these are narrower issues than B’s scheduling and accounting gaps.
